q: why do some people have photographic memory
people who struggle to remember names
a: True photographic memory (technically called eidetic memory) is extremely rare and involves the ability to recall images, sounds, or objects with high precision for a brief period after seeing them. Eidetic memory is most commonly observed in children, with estimates suggesting 2-10% of children may have eidetic abilities, but this usually fades with age. Most people who claim to have a photographic memory actually have exceptional but not perfect memory, often achieved through mnemonic techniques like the method of loci (memory palace), chunking, and spaced repetition. The term photographic memory is misleading because true eidetic memory is not a literal camera-like reproduction. Research suggests that eidetic memory may involve differences in brain structure and processing, particularly in the visual cortex and temporal lobes. The phenomenon of having a strong memory for some things while struggling with others is normal because memory is not a single faculty but a collection of different systems: short-term memory, working memory, long-term memory, episodic memory (for events), semantic memory (for facts), and procedural memory (for skills). Individual differences in these systems can vary greatly. Forgetting names is particularly common because names are arbitrary labels with no intrinsic meaning, making them harder to encode and retrieve than meaningful information.
